If companies rely on regulations to ensure market position then price gouging should be illegal (if say your water company decided to triple the price of water). This is referred to as regulatory capture if you're curious.

Instead of simple dollars, you add in time waiting (which actually makes it more expensive for wealthier people), and/or secondary markets. It's quite common for people to buy these products in a speculative fashion for resale eating the gap between true demand price (given a constant volume) and the store price. Restricting price only inserts volatility into the market. Then you end up with scenarios where soccer moms are prostituting themselves for the hot new toy (yes this actually happens). I'd rather they just raised the price at the store.

As far as companies that price gouge (to the extent that such a thing exists), I would determine if the new price was worth the commodity. If you really need the gas $10/gal would be worth it to me.

This caries it's own problems (namely increased shortages). The ability to charge higher prices incentivizes increased production and inventory.
